subtopics.title: Three Bills and Their Scope
subtopics.summary: The 130th Constitution Amendment Bill, 2025 is one of three Bills tabled by the Home Minister, and together the Bills propose the removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers under certain conditions. A Joint Parliamentary Committee is examining the Bill and is expected to finalise and adopt its report. The other two Bills are the Government of Union Territories (Amendment) Bill, 2025 and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2025.
facts: Introduced in 2025 as the 130th Constitution Amendment Bill
Three Bills tabled by the Home Minister
Bill 1: Constitution (One Hundred and Thirtieth Amendment) Bill, 2025
Bill 2: Government of Union Territories (Amendment) Bill, 2025
Bill 3: Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2025
The Bills propose removal of Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers under certain conditions
Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) is examining the 130th Amendment Bill
The JPC is expected to finalise and adopt its report

subtopics.title: Removal Conditions and Authorities
subtopics.summary: The Bill's trigger is arrest and detention for 30 consecutive days on an offence punishable with five years or more. The removal authority depends on the office: the President for Union Ministers, the Governor for State Ministers and Chief Ministers, and the Lieutenant Governor for Delhi and Jammu & Kashmir. If no advice is given for a Union Minister, the Minister automatically ceases to hold office on the 31st day.
facts: Trigger: arrested and detained for 30 consecutive days
The offence must be punishable with imprisonment of five years or more
Union Ministers: Article 75 is amended
Union Ministers: the President removes on the advice of the Prime Minister
If no advice is given, the Minister automatically ceases to hold office on the 31st day
A removed Minister can be reappointed after release from custody
State Ministers and Chief Ministers: Article 164, removal authority is the Governor
Delhi Ministers: Article 239AA, removal authority is the Lieutenant Governor
Union Territory Ministers: Government of Union Territories Act, 1963, removal authority is the Administrator or Lieutenant Governor
Jammu & Kashmir Ministers: J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019, removal authority is the Lieutenant Governor

subtopics.title: Governance Implications and Concerns
subtopics.summary: The Bill is presented as strengthening ethical governance by stopping leaders from holding power while facing serious criminal charges. It is also described as bridging a gap in the Representation of the People Act, which disqualifies legislators only after conviction. The booklet records several concerns, including misuse of arrests against opposition-led states, a threat to federalism and the presumption of innocence.
facts: The Bill upholds constitutional morality and ethical governance
It stops leaders from retaining power while facing serious criminal charges
It removes the 'governance from jail' anomaly
It protects public trust by acting against criminalisation of politics
It bridges a legal gap: the RPA disqualifies only post-conviction, while the Bill addresses interim arrests
Concern: the Centre could destabilise opposition-led states through targeted arrests
Concern: the Bill reduces the autonomy of elected state leaders, threatening federalism
Concern: removal based solely on detention contravenes 'innocent until proven guilty'
Concern: ED and CBI could be exploited to arrest leaders on weak charges

subtopics.title: Representation of People Act and Court Rulings
subtopics.summary: Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 sets different disqualification rules for convictions, depending on the offence and the sentence. Section 8(4), which protected sitting members who appeal within three months, was struck down by the Supreme Court. Supreme Court rulings on ministers with criminal backgrounds and on who can add grounds of disqualification form the wider legal background.
facts: Section 8(1): conviction for promoting enmity, rape, terrorist acts or insulting the national flag means six years' disqualification on mere conviction
Section 8(2): conviction for hoarding or dowry offences with a sentence of at least six months; the bar continues six years after release
Section 8(3): conviction for other offences with a sentence of not less than two years; disqualification till six years after release
Section 8(4): sitting MPs and MLAs can continue if they appeal within three months, until the term ends or the appeal is decided, whichever is earlier
Lily Thomas v. Union of India: the Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) as invalid
Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014): no constitutional bar exists on appointing ministers with a criminal background
Public Interest Foundation PIL (2018): only Parliament can legislate on disqualification; courts cannot add new grounds
V Senthil Balaji case (2025): a Tamil Nadu minister reappointed post-bail had to choose between freedom and office, and he stepped down while bail continued
Law Commission 170th Report: recommended disqualification at the framing of charges for offences punishable with five years or more

subtopics.title: Passage of a Constitution Amendment Bill
subtopics.summary: A Constitution amendment Bill can be introduced in either House, but it must be passed by both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Once passed, it is presented to the President, who is bound to give consent, and the Bill then becomes an Act. The booklet also links the process to the Anti-Defection Law and related constitutional articles.
facts: The Bill can be introduced either in Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
The Bill must be passed by both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Lok Sabha strength is 545 members
In a tie, the Presiding Officer of a house can cast his or her vote
The passed Bill is presented to the President
The President is bound to give consent
After assent the Bill becomes an Act
Related provisions: Articles 102 and 191, the Anti-Defection Law and the Lily Thomas case

quizzes.passage: The 130th Constitution Amendment Bill is part of a package of Bills that deal with removing leaders from office. Together, the Bills propose the removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers under certain conditions. The package reaches several levels of government, including the Union, the states and Delhi, so its rules are not limited to one office. The Bills set out the conditions for removal and name the authority that would act for each office. They also address whether a removed minister may later return to office after release. The Bills were presented as a set, and each one covers a different part of the framework. Each Bill has its own formal name, which the booklet lists in full. A committee is currently examining the main Bill, so the Bills remain under consideration. The rules differ between offices, so the scope of each one depends on the office involved. The booklet presents the conditions in a table that lists the offence threshold, the removal authority for each office and any additional provision. Comparing the rows of that table shows how the rules differ between the Union and the states. These details form the core of the proposal that the booklet describes.

quizzes.passage: The Bill is presented as a step toward ethical governance in public life. Supporters say it stops leaders from keeping power while facing serious charges, and that this protects public trust in institutions. It is also described as filling a gap in the law on legislators. The debate also brings in the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which sets out disqualification grounds for legislators. Supporters also point to the aim of closing constitutional gaps, which they say improves accountability in the executive. The booklet records these arguments under one heading and the concerns under another. Critics, however, have raised several concerns about how the provisions could work in practice. Their arguments focus on the position of elected state governments, on the rights of people who have been detained but not yet tried, and on the role of investigating agencies. Some critics also raise questions about the basic rights of an accused person. The concerns listed by critics are equally specific, and one of them is framed as a threat to federalism. These concerns mean the same provisions are seen in two ways, as a safeguard by some and as a risk by others. The booklet keeps both views in view, so the reader sees the reasons on each side.

Reason (R): The Bill addresses interim arrests, which the Representation of the People Act does not address.

quizzes.passage: Amending the Constitution follows a formal path that the booklet traces as a flow chart. A proposal is first drafted as a Bill and then introduced in Parliament. The Bill is then put to a vote, and the voting rules are more demanding than those for ordinary legislation. The booklet explains how the votes are counted and what happens when the count is level. The booklet sets out the vote thresholds for each House in its diagram. A Bill's stages are shown in order, and each stage has its own requirement, which differs for each House. After the chambers complete their votes, the Bill moves to the next stage in the process. The sequence ends with a formal step that follows the completion of the House stages. The booklet also connects this process with other parts of the Constitution and with case law on legislators. The chart includes a box listing the provisions and legal cases that relate to the process. The booklet presents the process with simple labels, so each step can be read on its own. The flow chart's steps are numbered, so the order of the process is easy to follow. A reader can compare the stages with the list of provisions in the box to see how the process connects to the wider law.
